Let \(h_n=t_n-t_{n-1}\), with
\[
h_n=
\begin{cases}
h,&n\equiv0\pmod3,\\
rh,&n\equiv1\pmod3,\\
r^2h,&n\equiv2\pmod3.
\end{cases}
\]
Since \(h\) only scales the derivative equation, set \(h=1\).

For a given phase \(a=n\bmod3\), define the backward node distances
\[
d_{a,j}=t_n-t_{n-j},\qquad j=1,2,3,4.
\]
They are
\[
\begin{aligned}
(d_{0,1},d_{0,2},d_{0,3},d_{0,4})
&=(1,1+r^2,1+r+r^2,2+r+r^2),\\
(d_{1,1},d_{1,2},d_{1,3},d_{1,4})
&=(r,1+r,1+r+r^2,2+r+r^2),\\
(d_{2,1},d_{2,2},d_{2,3},d_{2,4})
&=(r^2,r+r^2,1+r+r^2,1+r+2r^2).
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(b_{a,j}\) are the derivative weights of the interpolating polynomial, then
\[
b_{a,0}=\sum_{k=1}^4\frac1{d_{a,k}},
\]
and, for \(j\ge1\),
\[
b_{a,j}
=-\frac1{d_{a,j}}
\prod_{\substack{1\le k\le4\\k\ne j}}
\frac{d_{a,k}}{d_{a,k}-d_{a,j}}.
\]
The recurrence is
\[
\sum_{j=0}^4 b_{a,j}y_{n-j}=0,
\qquad a=n\bmod3.
\]

For a period multiplier \(\lambda\), write
\[
y_{3k+a}=\lambda^k x_a,\qquad a=0,1,2.
\]
Substitution gives a \(3\times3\) homogeneous system
\[
D_r(\lambda)x=0.
\]
The multiplier equation is therefore
\[
\det D_r(\lambda)=0.
\]

The constant solution gives \(\lambda=1\) for every \(r\). Applying the Schur-Cohn test to the remaining factor of \(\det D_r(\lambda)\), and simplifying, gives:

- all nonconstant multipliers satisfy \(|\lambda|<1\) precisely when \(Q(r)>0\);
- when \(Q(r)=0\), the only nonconstant multiplier on \(|\lambda|=1\) is
  \[
  \lambda=-1;
  \]
- for \(Q(r)<0\), one parasitic multiplier lies outside the unit circle.

Thus zero-stability is equivalent to \(Q(r)\ge0\).

Now
\[
Q(0)=-2<0,
\]
while \(Q(1)>0\). Moreover, every coefficient of \(Q'(r)\) is positive for \(r>0\), so \(Q\) is strictly increasing on \((0,\infty)\). Hence \(Q\) has exactly one zero in \((0,1)\), and the stable range is
\[
r_*\le r\le1.
\]

At \(r=r_*\), the parasitic period multiplier is \(\lambda=-1\).

\[
\boxed{r_*=\operatorname{root}_{(0,1)}Q}
\]
